read.sections.0.heading.source: Small actions can help a community
read.sections.0.heading.back: Small actions can help a community

read.sections.0.text.source: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to mean a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with a younger child, translate for someone who is new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to give their views on things that affect them. It also says children are free to start or join groups and to meet together.
read.sections.0.text.back: To contribute means to give time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing doesn't have to be a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner might read with younger children, translate for newcomers, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the community's work. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says children have the right to give their opinions on matters that affect them, and also that children are free to form or join groups and to meet.
read.sections.0.text.note: Here the English names the treaty, so it is อนุสัญญาว่าด้วยสิทธิเด็กของสหประชาชาติ (Lesson 19 says ข้อตกลง because its English says 'agreement'). 'campaign' is การรณรงค์.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: To contribute is to give your time or help to make things better. You do not need to do something big. Small acts help a community too. You can read with a young child. You can translate for a new learner. You can clean a room you share. You can join a club. The United Nations has a list of rights for children. It says children can give their views. It also says they can join groups.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Contributing is giving time or help to make things better. You don't have to do something big. Small actions can help a community too. You can read with young children. You can translate for new learners. You can clean a shared room. You can join a club. The United Nations has a list of children's rights. This list says children can give their opinions, and it says children can join groups.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: Second pass: "It says children can give their views" had no subject after the space (บอกว่า... read as if the UN sentence went on); now รายการนี้บอกว่า... ("this list says").

read.sections.1.heading.source: Start with evidence and work together
read.sections.1.heading.back: Start with evidence and work together

read.sections.1.text.source: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed litter near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, might upset people and would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
read.sections.1.text.back: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed rubbish near the bus stop in front of the centre. They had three ideas. Idea 1 is to post an angry message online, which might upset people and doesn't solve the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence: learners go with a teacher to ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
read.sections.1.text.note: stakeholder = ผู้มีส่วนเกี่ยวข้อง (KEY_TERMS, check); defined in the text as คนที่ได้รับผลจากปัญหา. 'bus users' is คนที่ใช้รถเมล์ / คนใช้รถเมล์.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some learners saw litter near a bus stop. They had three ideas. Idea 1 was an angry post. It would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask bus users what is missing. Stakeholders are people who are affected by a problem. Bus users are stakeholders. So is the centre manager. Idea 3 is a short, polite letter to the manager. It asks for a new bin.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A group of learners saw rubbish near the bus stop. They had three ideas. Idea 1 is to post an angry message, which doesn't solve the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. Learners go with a teacher to ask bus users what is missing. Stakeholders are people affected by a problem. Bus users are stakeholders. So is the centre manager. Idea 3 is a short, polite letter to the manager asking for a new bin.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Do it safely and look back

read.sections.2.text.source: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take a photo of the litter, it should not show anyone's face or private information. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was included? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
read.sections.2.text.back: Good contributing must be safe. Before the clean-up, the learners talk with a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and rubbish bags, and arrange for someone to dispose of the rubbish. If they take photos of the rubbish, the photos shouldn't show anyone's face or personal information. You don't need to speak in public, post online or put yourself in danger to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who took part? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
read.sections.2.text.note: permission = การอนุญาต. The glossary needs the exact letters in both texts, so the reading says ได้รับการอนุญาต / ให้การอนุญาต, a little more formal than ได้รับอนุญาต. The three look-back questions keep their question marks.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk to a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where the rubbish goes. A photo must not show faces. You do not need to speak in public or post online. After you help, look back. What changed? Who was included? What can be better next time?
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Helping must be safe. First, the learners talk with a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and rubbish bags. They plan where the rubbish will go. Photos must not show people's faces. You don't have to speak in public or post online. After helping, look back. What changed? Who took part? What could be better next time?

write.example.source: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask users if they see a change.
write.example.back: Our goal is to make the bus stop in front of our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. We will go with a teacher to ask five bus users. We will ask permission from the teacher and the centre manager to organise a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to dispose of. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask bus users if they see a change.

watch.afterQuestion.source: What help do young people need so that adults listen to their ideas?
watch.afterQuestion.back: What help do youth need so that adults listen to their ideas?

watch.summary.source: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to young people and to act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not have to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with a younger child or keeping a shared space clean.
watch.summary.back: In this UNICEF video, youth send a message to world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places they live. They ask leaders to listen to youth and take action. The video shows that youth have good ideas about problems that affect them, but ideas need to reach the right people. For that to happen, youth need facts, help from adults and real chances to change what happens. You don't need to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, such as reading with younger children or keeping a shared space clean.
